title: Is Full-Time Teaching Sustainable? Cognitive Load, Task-Switching, and the Reality of Part-Time Work
author: Dr Dario Emanuele
summary: Emanuele argues that the full-time secondary teaching timetable is cognitively unsustainable, and that the drift toward part-time contracts is a symptom of a job design problem rather than a failure of teacher resilience. He applies Cognitive Load Theory, usually used to structure student learning, to teachers themselves, showing how intrinsic, extraneous and germane demands pile up across a day of rapid context switches. He adds the idea of attention residue, where thoughts from one class drag on working memory in the next, so that by the fifth period executive function is depleted. He then examines the part-time paradox: split classes create inconsistency in routines, behaviour enforcement and diagnostic feedback, while part-time teachers often use their unpaid day to finish planning and marking. He closes with three redesign proposals: protected preparation time and fewer contact hours, centralised and fully resourced curricula, and timetables built around human cognitive limits.
points: Teacher burnout is framed as a predictable consequence of timetable design, since rapid context switching leaves attention residue and no time for cognitive reset.
Cognitive Load Theory applies to teachers as well as students, with intrinsic, extraneous and germane loads all active at once in every lesson.
Part-time contracts are often a self-preservation strategy in which teachers effectively take a pay cut to buy back the unpaid time their work requires.
Split classes carry real costs in routine consistency, behaviour enforcement and the diagnostic continuity that lets one teacher spot misconceptions early.
Proposed fixes are protected non-contact windows after heavy blocks, shared fully resourced curricula, and timetables that minimise room swaps and multi-key-stage jumps.
quotes: If you look closely at a secondary school teacher’s daily timetable, you will see an operational schedule that defies and overloads human cognitive architecture.
What we rarely admit is that Cognitive Load Theory applies just as forcefully to teachers as it does to students.
The brain does not cleanly wipe its working memory clean when the lesson bell rings; residual thoughts from the previous class continuously drag on working memory capacity during the next.
By period five, executive function is depleted. This is not a personal failure of resilience; it is a predictable biological outcome.

In essence, teachers are taking a 20% pay cut simply to buy back the working time necessary to perform their job to a professional standard without collapsing from exhaustion. They are subsidising a broken system with their own salary.

A single teacher tracking a student’s progress over four consecutive lessons notices subtle patterns of misconception early. Split teaching disrupts this continuous feedback loop, making responsive teaching far harder to coordinate effectively.

Teaching will always be a demanding, high-energy profession. But until we recognise that human cognitive energy is a finite resource, we will continue to lose brilliant teachers to burnout, or force them to pay out of their own pockets for the time it takes to survive.
